mcqs.question: What assumption does LRU replacement make about which line is safest to evict?
options: The line that was loaded first is safest to evict
The line with the smallest tag value is least useful
The line accessed longest ago is least likely to be accessed again soon, based on temporal locality
A randomly chosen line is just as safe as any other
mcqs.explanation: LRU is a direct bet on temporal locality: recently-used data tends to be reused soon, so the line untouched longest is the best guess for "won't be needed again soon." Load order (that's FIFO) and tag value have no bearing on LRU's decision.

mcqs.question: Why don't high-associativity caches implement exact LRU tracking in hardware?
options: Exact LRU is illegal under most ISA specifications
LRU can only be implemented for direct-mapped caches
Exact LRU would violate cache coherence protocols
The number of possible recency orderings grows combinatorially with associativity, making exact tracking bits impractically expensive
mcqs.explanation: An N-way set has N! possible recency orderings; representing that exactly needs bits that grow much faster than N, so real hardware uses cheap approximations (clock, pseudo-LRU) instead. LRU has nothing to do with ISA legality, coherence protocols, or direct-mapped caches (which have no replacement decision to make at all).

mcqs.question: In a 4-way LRU set with contents (most- to least-recent) D, A, C, B, a new access misses. Which line is evicted?
options: B, because it sits at the least-recently-used end of the ordering
D, because it was the most recently used
The evicted line is chosen randomly among all four
mcqs.explanation: LRU always evicts whichever way is currently at the least-recently-used end of the tracked order — here, B. Alphabetical order and randomness play no role in true LRU; only recency of access matters.

mcqs.question: Why is Belady's optimal (MIN) replacement policy never used in a real cache?
options: It has a worse hit rate than LRU on most workloads
It requires knowing the future sequence of accesses, which is unavailable to hardware in real time
It only works for fully associative caches
It requires more comparator hardware than any real policy could afford
mcqs.explanation: Belady's MIN evicts the line that will be used furthest in the future — provably optimal, but only computable with perfect foresight of the access stream, which no online cache has. It's used purely as a theoretical upper bound to measure real policies like LRU against, and it isn't restricted to fully associative caches or unusually hardware-hungry.
